summary.title: How Physics Engines Work
summary.one_liner: You learn the core math behind a 2D game physics engine: vectors, Newton's second law, numerical integration (Euler and Velocity Verlet), rigid-body rotation, and collision detection with the separating axis theorem.
keywords: build a physics engine in javascript
takeaways: Model points and forces as vectors so one set of math handles x, y and rotation together.
Simulate motion by summing forces, applying F = ma, then integrating acceleration to velocity and position each timestep.
Velocity Verlet is more accurate and stable than the simple Euler method for numerical integration.
Rotation uses angle, angular velocity, moment of inertia and torque (the cross product of force and displacement).
Collision detection is split into broad phase (grids, quadtrees, AABB) and narrow phase; the separating axis theorem tests convex polygons by checking projection overlap on each side's axis.
summary.summary: The article, by Burak Kanber on Build New Games, teaches the essential physics behind game engines rather than a step-by-step build guide. It argues for using vector math for points, velocities and forces, then derives Newton's second law and the steps to simulate motion. It explains Euler and Velocity Verlet integration with pseudocode, and includes JSFiddle-based checkpoints on air drag, springs and damping. The later sections cover rigid-body rotation (torque, moment of inertia) and collision detection, focusing on the separating axis theorem for convex 2D polygons.
